story_text.value:
Hi HN, excited to be open sourcing two tools that we have built over past few months which helps to understand your own work with AI coding agents

Agent Desk is a local macOS app which allows you to browse your sessions across all top coding agents - Claude code, cursor, codex, github copilot, Kiro, Antigravity. You can find sessions by your projects, revisit those conversations, understand and inspect your entire harness - rules, skills, hooks, subagents.

https://github.com/tetriz-ai/agent-desk

Session Intelligence is a go library which helps structure and analyse your session transcripts using your own LLM. It can help understand missing context, repeated corrections, if session reached its goal and where is effort being wasted. It can also surface leaked credentials and PII.

https://github.com/tetriz-ai/session-intelligence

Both are MIT-licensed.

You can also combine both together and understanding your agent steering habits better.

Excited about the community using it.

story_text.value:
Hi Hacker News, I'm Harjot. I've been using Meta's Muse Code CLI daily for a few weeks now. One thing that I found difficult to handle was managing or controlling multiple sessions across multiple projects, while using the terminal for the muse CLI. Initially, I used cmux to create workspaces/groups for my different projects to group them, and then created 4 split terminals in each of those projects, that ran muse code sessions in each of them. It worked, but it was ugly. I didn't like using that. It could be because I'm not really a terminal person and would much rather prefer a proper dedicated GUI or desktop/app interface, and I would prefer it any time over a terminal screen or CLI. So it might be personal preference but yeah.

So, I started building a desktop app around it, mainly to scratch my own itch.

Helicon is a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus a VS Code extension that also works in Cursor and Devin. It doesn't replace the CLI. It runs `muse serve` and talks to it, and it reuses your existing `muse login`, so you don't have to get an API key and you don't pay an extra bill. You can use your existing Muse Code subscription plans.

Some things that I use the most: 1. Resuming sessions that I started in the terminal. I don't start many sessions in the terminal now that Helicon exists, but initially I wanted to access all the sessions that were running in a terminal to be accessible from Helicon, when it was created initially. 2. Inline diffs that I can approve, similar to how Cursor works. 3. I can clearly see my 5-hour and weekly plan limits directly from the app itself and don't have to manually keep going to Meta's Muse Code billing page and manually keep refreshing the page to see my current usage/limits.

I built it using Tauri 2 and React. It is MIT licensed. I built a lot of it with AI coding agents, especially Opus 5.5 (I really like using this model). It's at v0.21.9 now, and 9 people have contributed so far.

Some issues: the Windows installer isn't code-signed yet, so you'll see a SmartScreen warning. And the macOS build isn't notarized, so you need to click "Open Anyway" once.

You can try it in the browser with mock data, no install needed: https://helicon.sh/try

It's unofficial and not affiliated with Meta.

If you use a coding CLI every day, what would you want from a GUI for it? And what would make you go back to the terminal?

title.value: Show HN: Helicon – Desktop App for Meta's Muse Code CLI (Linux, Windows, macOS)

story_text.value:
About 11 months ago i revived the amazing but unfortunately unmaintained spotify-tui. Since then I have been working on it almost non stop, finding a lot of problems on the way.

One of the main issues I ran into were the Spotify web API rate limits. Third party clients like spotatui are dependent on a developer app made in the Spotify developer dashboard, which get rate limited a lot and Spotify has slowly been deprecating endpoints from it. The workaround for this used to be using a shared client id from ncspot but unfortunately that got rate limited too. This is when i started adding other playback sources, including YouTube, Navidrome/Subsonic, Internet radio with +- 30.000 stations, local files, Qobuz for lossless audio and Apple Music for macOS only where it controls the music app remotely.

I fixed both the deprecated endpoints and the rate limits with one solution. It still uses librespot in the back, my spotatui specific fork, but gets all data from it instead of only playback. The data comes from the internal API of the official clients, that API gives metadata, playlists, the user library, devices, lyrics and audio analysis. For searching it uses Pathfinder, the internal GraphQL API.

There are no web API rate limits because there is no shared app quota. Every user uses their own session as if it was the official client. The only potential problem is that Spotify does not document this API so any change on their side would break it. I intend to fix any of those issues as soon as they pop up.

It all started as a TUI back in 2019 but since then I've added a GUI to it too. The GUI is still a bit behind the TUI in terms of features, it only ships Spotify for now, but full parity between the TUI and GUI is coming soon. After that full parity with the official client is next. That is also why I made the GUI looks almost the same as the official client. That way its easier for me and users to find missing features.

Spotatui also has lua scripting support, a optional Web companion on spotatui.com, and if you have a AI coding agent like ChatGPT codex or Claude Code you can enable the MCP tools, which lets AI become your personal DJ just by talking to it.

Its written in Rust, uses ratatui for the terminal UI and Tauri 2 for the GUI. The Rust core starts a small web server with localhost that only your pc can reach which the GUI then serves. Both frontends share the same playback logic, the same login and the same Spotify code. The only difference is how you interact with it.

On first launch it opens a web browser where you need to login with your Spotify premium account (premium is not optional), that is the whole setup done. I would love any feedback about bugs you encounter or features you would like to see. GitHub: https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui Releases: https://github.com/LargeModGames/spotatui/releases/latest Website: https://spotatui.com/

Thanks to librespot for making this all possible

title.value: Show HN: Spotatui, a Spotify TUI/GUI without web API rate limits
